title: Eternal life is God’s greatest gift to those who endure
setting: In late May or early June 1829, David Whitmer drove his wagon to Harmony, Pennsylvania. He moved Joseph Smith and Oliver Cowdery to his father Peter Whitmer Sr.’s farm in Fayette, New York. There Joseph worked to finish translating the Book of Mormon. David and his brothers John and Peter Jr. became eager helpers and wanted to know their duties. Joseph’s history says he asked the Lord through the Urim and Thummim, and this revelation for David came first. Its wording suggests David had already been baptized that month.
summary: The revelation opens with the same words given to Joseph Knight and others: a marvelous work is about to come forth. It says the field is ready to harvest and whoever reaps is called. It tells David to seek to establish Zion and keep the commandments in all things. If he endures to the end, he will have eternal life, the greatest gift of God. If he asks the Father in faith, he will receive the Holy Ghost. The Spirit will help him witness what he hears and sees and declare repentance. The speaker names himself Jesus Christ and says the gospel must go from the Gentiles to Israel. It ends by telling David he is called to assist and will be blessed if faithful.

contextNote.title: The greatest gift comes at the end
contextNote.text: David wanted to know what his part in the work should be. Verse 7 sets the long goal before the near task. Keeping the commandments and enduring to the end lead to eternal life. The verse ranks that gift “the greatest of all the gifts of God,” above every other. Verse 8 then names a nearer gift, the Holy Ghost, given so David can “stand as a witness” and declare repentance. The order matters: the Spirit equips the witness now, and endurance brings the final gift. In this passage, to “endure” means keeping commandments over a whole life, not for a season.

ldsText: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 12–17 shows the Lord answering people who sincerely ask about their part. Verse 8 says David would “stand as a witness” of what he would “hear and see”; how did that promise come true in section 17?
reviewNote: Read all 11 verses. Official heading gives Fayette, June 1829, to David Whitmer, through the Urim and Thummim, followed by sections 15 and 16. JSP historical introduction read for the move from Harmony, the Whitmer brothers’ inquiry, and David’s baptism in mid-June. The precise date of the move (late May or early June) is uncertain. Verse 11 calls him “David”; Whitmer later became one of the Three Witnesses. Fact-check 2026-10-12: setting now attributes the Urim and Thummim inquiry to Joseph’s history (historical voice). Other facts confirmed against heading and JSP.
